title: Monolith vs Microservices
subtitle: Watch one checkout move from a single codebase to separate services, and see what you gain and what the network costs.
learn: What a monolith and a modular monolith are, and why the second is often the better start
How to draw service boundaries around business capabilities, not technical layers
Why each service must own its data, and what you give up (joins, easy transactions)
The costs of distribution: latency, partial failure, availability that multiplies, harder debugging
When splitting is worth it and when it is premature

steps.title: One app does everything
steps.body: Picture a small online shop built as one program, called a monolith. Checkout, orders, payments and stock all live inside it and share one database. When one part needs another, it just calls a function, which is fast and simple. The animation shows one checkout request saved in a single transaction, a group of database changes that all succeed or all fail together. Now the team grows from 5 to 50 people. Should we break this program up, and what would it cost?
steps.idea: A monolith is one program deployed as a unit: its internal calls are cheap and one transaction covers everything.
steps.caption: The whole checkout runs inside one program and one database.

steps.title: Modular monolith first
steps.body: Before splitting anything over the network, split the code. A modular monolith is still one program, but it is divided into modules such as orders and payments. Each module offers a small public interface and keeps its own tables, and other modules must not read those tables directly. The animation shows both modules saving data in one transaction. Calls stay in one process, so there is no network cost, but it still deploys and scales as one unit. Enforce the rules with build checks, or the boundaries slowly fade.
steps.idea: Clean module boundaries inside one program give much of the design benefit of microservices without the network cost.
steps.caption: One program, one database, but each module uses only its own tables.

steps.title: Draw boundaries by capability
steps.body: When one team or module really needs to ship on its own, pull it out as a separate service. Cut along business capabilities such as orders, payments or catalog, not technical layers like 'all the controllers'. A good boundary changes for one reason and belongs to one team. The animation sends checkout through the API gateway (the single front door that routes each request to the right service) to a new Orders service, which saves order 4821 in its own database. There is still one internal hop, so checkout stays at about 30 ms.
steps.idea: A good service matches one business capability and one team, so most changes touch only one service.
steps.caption: The gateway now sends checkout to the Orders service, which saves order 4821.

steps.title: Each service owns its data
steps.body: Each service owns its data. Payments has its own database, and only the Payments service may read or write it. Everyone else must ask through its API. In the animation, Orders asks Payments to charge order 4821 and Payments saves it in its own database, but Orders reading that database directly is blocked. This lets Payments change its tables freely. The price: you can no longer join orders to payments in one SQL query or wrap both writes in one transaction. Sharing a database would quietly rebuild the monolith. Checkout now spans three boxes, so it gets slower and less available (next step).
steps.idea: Owning its data is what makes a service independent; a shared database ties services back together.
steps.caption: Orders must ask Payments through its API; reading Payments' database directly is blocked.

steps.title: A function call became a network call
steps.body: A function call inside one program takes well under a microsecond. A network round trip in one data center takes about 0.5 to 2 ms, plus serializing (turning data into bytes), TLS encryption and routing. Checkout gains one hop, and Payments writes to its own database, so it grows from about 30 to 36 ms here. Availability falls too. Say each box, database included, is up 99.9% of the time. Gateway plus one app gives about 99.8% (17.5 hours down a year). Gateway, Orders and Payments give 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999, about 99.7% (26 hours), if failures are independent. Pass a trace ID along every call, since one checkout now logs in three places.
steps.idea: Every network hop adds delay and a new way to fail, and the availability of chained services multiplies.
steps.caption: Checkout now crosses three boxes, so it is slower and less available.

steps.title: No cross-service transaction
steps.body: In the monolith, the order and the payment were saved in one transaction. Now they sit in two databases, so one transaction cannot cover both. One fix: Orders saves the order, publishes an OrderPlaced event to a queue (a waiting line for messages) and replies 202 Accepted at once. Payments picks the event up later and charges. Checkout answers faster (about 32 ms) and does not fail just because Payments is down, but the queue is now a dependency, and the data is only eventually consistent: for a while the order exists but is unpaid. The Outbox and Idempotency lessons cover keeping save and publish in step, and charging once.
steps.idea: Splitting data trades one all-or-nothing transaction for eventual consistency, which you must design around.
steps.caption: Orders queues OrderPlaced and answers; Payments handles it a moment later.

steps.title: Payments gets slow
steps.body: Now suppose Payments gets slow, taking 3 seconds per call because its card provider is struggling, and Orders has set no timeout (a limit on how long to wait). Orders keeps waiting. Each waiting request holds a thread, a worker that handles one job at a time, so Orders soon runs out of free threads and stops serving anyone. One slow service has dragged down its caller: a cascading failure. The defences are short timeouts, limited retries and circuit breakers (which pause calls to a failing service). The Timeouts and Retries lesson covers them.
steps.idea: In a distributed system a slow dependency can be as dangerous as a dead one, because callers pile up waiting.
steps.caption: Orders is stuck waiting on a slow Payments and runs out of threads.

steps.title: When splitting pays off
steps.body: Microservices give you independent deploys, independent scaling and team autonomy. These matter when many teams keep colliding in one codebase, or when one part has very different load from the rest. The cost is harder debugging across services, versioned APIs, many build pipelines and on-call duty for more moving parts. As a rough rule of thumb, one team or a handful of engineers is usually faster with a well-structured modular monolith. The highlighted boxes show the two shapes of the same checkout.
steps.idea: Split because of a specific pain, such as team contention or scaling, not because microservices sound modern.
steps.caption: Same checkout, two shapes: one program, or separate services.

steps.title: Monolith, modular, or micro
steps.body: A monolith is simple and fast inside. A modular monolith keeps that speed while enforcing clean boundaries. Microservices cut along business capabilities and give each service its own data, which allows independent deploys and scaling. The price is network delay, partial failures, lower combined availability, no easy cross-service transaction and harder debugging. So start modular, and split only on purpose.
steps.idea: Boundaries first, network second: make the modules clean before you make them remote.
steps.caption: Orders and Payments run separately, each with its own database.

quiz.q: A team wants cleaner code boundaries but has 8 engineers and one product. What is usually the best first move?
options: Build a modular monolith with enforced module interfaces
Give every module direct access to every table
Move all data into one shared service database
quiz.why: A modular monolith gives clear boundaries and ownership without network calls or distributed transactions, which a small team does not need yet.

quiz.q: Orders and Payments are separate services, but both read and write the same database tables. What is the main problem?
options: They cannot be deployed at all
The database will refuse more than one client
A schema change in one can break the other, so they are not truly independent
quiz.why: Shared tables couple the services at the data level. Independent deploys and schema changes need each service to own its data and expose it only through an API.

quiz.q: A request passes through a gateway and two services in a chain, each 99.9% available with its database counted inside. Roughly what is the availability of the whole chain?
quiz.why: Availabilities in series multiply: 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999 is about 0.997, so every extra hard dependency lowers the total.

quiz.q: Which split follows a good service boundary?
options: A Payments service owned by one team that changes for payment reasons
A controllers service, a models service, and a views service
A Catalog service per database table that every team shares
One service per developer, each owning a slice of every feature
quiz.why: Good boundaries follow business capabilities with a single owning team. Technical layers force almost every feature to change all services at once.

quiz.q: After extracting Payments, Orders calls it synchronously and Payments becomes very slow. What can happen if Orders has no timeout?
options: Orders automatically fails fast because the platform adds timeouts
Orders threads pile up waiting, and Orders starts failing too
Nothing, because slow is not a failure
quiz.why: Waiting callers hold threads and connections. Without timeouts the slowness cascades upstream and takes the caller down as well.

cheatsheet.def: One deployable unit containing all features, usually with a single database. Simple to build, test, and run; scales and deploys as a whole.
A monolith divided into modules with explicit interfaces and private data. Gives clear boundaries without network calls.
The line around a business capability owned by one team. Good boundaries change for one reason and need few cross-service calls.
Each service alone reads and writes its data; others use its API. Enables independent change but removes joins and shared transactions.
Roughly 0.5 to 2 ms inside a data center, versus nanoseconds in-process, plus serialization and new failure modes.
Multiply the availabilities of hard dependencies, assuming independent failures: gateway, Orders and Payments at 99.9% each give about 99.7%.
A slow or failing service exhausts its callers' threads, spreading the outage upstream. Fight it with timeouts and circuit breakers.
Data in separate stores agrees after a short delay rather than instantly. The usual price of splitting data across services.
